questions.q: What's the key difference between environment: and env_file: in a compose.yaml service?
options: environment: lists variables inline in the file itself; env_file: points at a separate file whose contents get loaded as variables
They are two names for exactly the same feature
environment: only works for numbers; env_file: only works for strings
env_file: deletes all previously set environment variables
questions.explain: environment: puts values directly in compose.yaml, while env_file: loads them from a separate file -- usually a gitignored .env holding real, sensitive values.

questions.q: Where does Compose mount a secret inside a container by default?
options: As an environment variable, the same as env_file:
As a file under /run/secrets/<secret name>
Nowhere -- secrets are only visible to the Compose CLI on the host
In the container's /etc/passwd file
questions.explain: Compose secrets are mounted as files at /run/secrets/<name> inside the container, rather than being injected as environment variables.

questions.q: Why shouldn't Northbridge commit its real .env file, with live Stripe keys and database passwords, to git?
options: Committed files are automatically encrypted by GitHub, so there's no real risk
Anyone with access to the repository's history would be able to read every secret in plain text, indefinitely
Git doesn't support filenames that start with a dot
Compose refuses to start if .env is tracked by git
questions.explain: Once a secret is committed, it's in the repository's history forever, readable by anyone with access to that history, even if the file is later deleted.

questions.q: What's the purpose of a committed .env.example file alongside a gitignored .env?
options: It documents which variables are needed, with placeholder or empty values, without exposing real secrets
It's a backup copy of the real secrets in case .env is lost
It's required by Docker Compose before any container can start
It automatically generates random secrets for production use
questions.explain: .env.example tells every developer which variables the app expects, without ever containing a real, sensitive value.

questions.q: In production, where should real secret values typically come from instead of a checked-in file?
options: Hardcoded directly into the Dockerfile
The hosting platform's own secret or environment-variable injection, never the repository
Printed in the application's log output for the team to copy
A public gist for easy sharing
questions.explain: Production secrets should come from the platform's own secret management or environment injection -- the repository itself should never contain real secret values.
